name: Emai
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 6 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Schaefer, Ronald P. & Francis O. Egbokhare. 2022. Secondary concepts and internal dynamics of Emai Serial Verb Constructions. Stellenbosch Papers in Linguistics Plus 65: 233-265. doi:10.5842/65-1-976 (open access, CC BY 4.0; publisher PDF saved)
catalog_locator: p. 234, Section 1 Introduction, second paragraph; orthography note under 'Abbreviations', p. 262
catalog_quote: Emai is a minor language in the Edoid group (Elugbe 1989). It is spoken in over 10 villages with approximately 20-25,000 speakers. A tonal language, Emai shows lexical and grammatical tones high (ˊ), low (ˋ), and downstep high (ˊ'). Its morphological template for the basic verb is X-stem-Y. X identifies a persistive qualifier prefix and Y encompasses contrasting perfective/ imperfective toneme suffixes. Tones from these suffixes spread onto lexically toneless verbs. The imperfective suffix is a floating low tone. Traces of perfective suffix -í and its high tone are evident in simple clauses with an intransitive verb or a monotransitive verb whose direct object has left dislocated. ... [p. 262] Orthographic conventions reflect those in Schaefer and Egbokhare (1999; 2007; 2017), where o represents a half open back vowel, e a half open front vowel, and vb a voiced bilabial approximant. For tone, acute accent marks high, grave accent signals low, and acute accent followed by an apostrophe designates high downstep.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Emai (the described lect of Emai-Iuleha-Ora, of which Ihievbe is a section) is a tone language with lexical and grammatical H, L and downstepped H; nouns carry lexical tone, verbs are lexically toneless and take tone from aspect suffixes. The authors say nothing about word stress or accent in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: none (verbs and personal pronouns are toneless/construction-dependent per Egbokhare 1989 fn.3)
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns lexical/grammatical tone at word and clause level in Emai; no stress domain is described. Applies to Ihievbe only by virtue of Glottolog/Ethnologue treating Ihievbe as a section of the same language.
new_statements.identity_note: ihie1238 Ihievbe [ihi] is a Glottolog Bookkeeping entry: 'rather a section of the Emai-Iuleha-Ora [ema] language' (emai1241; Glottolog cites Elugbe 1989:16, Jungraithmayr & Ganslmayr 1986:34, Lewis 2013:95-96). Older Ethnologue editions (2005, 2009) instead filed Ihievbe under North-Central Edoid, Ghotuo-Uneme-Yekhee. Egbokhare 2011:67-69 lists Ihievbe among lects Elugbe left unclassified and reports Oyakhire 1997's dialect group A = Emai, Ihievbe, Ora, Iuleha, Ievbu, Uokha, Urore, Ohami, Sobe; the Emai dictionary glosses Ihievbe as the village 'immediately northeast of Emailand'. The quoted statement describes the Emai lect (Schaefer & Egbokhare's fieldwork variety, Afuze area), not Ihievbe speech itself; no Ihievbe-specific description exists. If catalogued, the entry should be keyed to emai1241 (or flagged as inherited from it).

new_statements.quote: 2.3 Tonal features Emai is a terraced-level tone language showing high, low, and downstepped high. For some word classes, inherent tone values distinguish words that in all [...] Various combinations of tone occur within lexical items. An initial high tone can be followed by a low tone, a high tone, or a down stepped high, the latter being one step lower [...] orthographic practice, high tone is represented by an acute accent, low tone by a grave accent, and down stepped high by an acute accent immediately [...]

tone_statements.citation: Egbokhare, Oisaghaede Francis. 1990. A Phonology of Emai. PhD dissertation, University of Ibadan. xvii+396 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Emai is a terraced level tone language with two basic tones, high (H) and low (L). These tones contrast as shown in the examples below: 1 a) ɔ̀kpá 'one' b) ɔ̀kpà 'cock' c) òí 'pomade' d) óì 'thief' ... Emai exhibits downstep (both automatic and non-automatic) in both lexical items and in constructions - affecting both high and low tones. ... At the systematic phonetic level Emai has the following tones: high, low, downstep high, downstep low, downglide, rising and falling tones.
tone_statements.summary: Two basic level tones H, L with terracing; downstepped H and L; falling/rising contours derived by glide formation/elision (6.1.4); elided L floats; tense/aspect marked by tonal melodies.

tone_statements.quote: In the Edoid language Emai, metatony signals the relational nature of a verb to an immediately following constituent. The principal exponent is segmental suffix -i and its tone values, high or low. As a mark of perfective (PFV) aspect, -í spreads its high tone over a preceding toneless verb stem after which tone and segment dissolve or remain intact, depending on their immediately following constituent. [...] We illustrate patterns of Emai metatony with bivalent verbs gbe 'hit' and o 'enter.' Both are lexically toneless, as is the norm for verbs throughout Edoid (Elugbe 1989).
tone_statements.check: quotation from a journal article located by the 2026-09-24 journal search, not yet verified by a second reading
tone_statements.summary: The paper shows Emai as a high/low tone language with downstep in which verbs are lexically toneless and the perfective suffix -í carries a high tone that spreads onto the verb, staying high before an adjunct, turning low clause-finally, and being suppressed before an argument (metatony). This confirms the catalog's lexical-tone classification and adds the detail that verb tone is grammatical rath

sources.citation: Schaefer, Ronald P. & Egbokhare, Francis O. 2021. Metatony, S-constituent linkage, and cognate objects. Proceedings of the Linguistic Society of America 6(1): 641-648. doi:10.3765/plsa.v6i1.5000
sources.quote: In the Edoid language Emai, metatony signals the relational nature of a verb to an immediately following constituent. The principal exponent is segmental suffix -i and its tone values, high or low. As a mark of perfective (PFV) aspect, -í spreads its high tone over a preceding toneless verb stem after which tone and segment dissolve or remain intact, depending on their immediately following constituent. [...] We illustrate patterns of Emai metatony with bivalent verbs gbe 'hit' and o 'enter.' Both are lexically toneless, as is the norm for verbs throughout Edoid (Elugbe 1989).
sources.note: Analyses metatony in Emai: the perfective suffix -i carries underlying high tone, retained as high before adjuncts, low clause-finally, and prohibited before verb arguments, with an asymmetry between two verb classes before S-constituents and cognate objects.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the Linguistic Society of America

tone.quote: Emai is a terraced level tone language with two basic tones, high (H) and low (L). These tones contrast as shown in the examples below: 1 a) ɔ̀kpá 'one' b) ɔ̀kpà 'cock' c) òí 'pomade' d) óì 'thief' ... Emai exhibits downstep (both automatic and non-automatic) in both lexical items and in constructions - affecting both high and low tones. ... At the systematic phonetic level Emai has the following tones: high, low, downstep high, downstep low, downglide, rising and falling tones.
tone.summary: Two basic level tones H, L with terracing; downstepped H and L; falling/rising contours derived by glide formation/elision (6.1.4); elided L floats; tense/aspect marked by tonal melodies.
